en: Homage to the Buddha! Having paid homage to the author of this treatise, the son of the Sugata, [I shall compose this work].
And I shall strive to explain the meaning to those such as ourselves, for the sake of discerning the truth.
[The Body of the Treatise] Therein, first of all, the body of the treatise is established:
the characteristics, the obscurations, reality, and the cultivation of the antidote.
And therein lie the abiding, the attainment of the fruit, and indeed the supremacy of the vehicle.
Thus, these seven topics are taught in this treatise; namely:

characteristics, obscurations, reality, the cultivation of the antidote, the stages within that very cultivation of the antidote, the attainment of the fruit, and the supremacy of the vehicle as the seventh topic.
Regarding that, concerning its characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), he says: [1. Unreal imagination; a. Its characteristic as existence and non-existence].
Unreal imagination exists; duality is not found there.
But emptiness exists here, and within that, it [unreal imagination] also exists. (1.1)
In this context, "unreal imagination" (abhūtaparikalpa) is the conceptualization of the grasped and the grasper;
"the two" refers to the grasped and the grasper;
and "emptiness" is that unreal imagination's being devoid of the state of grasped and grasper.
In that [emptiness] as well, that [unreal imagination] exists;

thus, one correctly perceives that whatever is not present in something is empty of that, and one understands according to reality that what remains there truly exists here. In this way, the non-erroneous characteristic of emptiness is elucidated.
Therefore, everything is described as neither empty nor non-empty;
because of existence, non-existence, and again existence, that is the middle way.
It is not empty because of emptiness and because of the imagination of the unreal.
Nor is it non-empty with respect to the duality of the apprehended object and the apprehending subject;
for everything— both that which is conditioned, known as "unreal imagination," and that which is unconditioned, known as "emptiness"— is [thus characterized].

It is prescribed and indicated that, because the unreal imagination exists, because duality does not exist, and because emptiness exists within the unreal imagination and the unreal imagination exists within that [emptiness], that is the middle way;
for it is all of this.
It is neither exclusively empty nor exclusively non-empty;
thus, this reading is made consistent with the *Prajñāpāramitā* and other texts, which state that "all this is neither empty nor non-empty.
[b. Svalakṣaṇa]
Having thus explained the characteristic of existence and the characteristic of non-existence of unreal imagination,
he explains its own characteristic:
"It arises as the appearance of objects, sentient beings, self, and representations."
Consciousness does not have an object; because that [object] is absent, it too is non-existent.
(I.3) In this context, that which appears as an object is what manifests in the form of visible matter (*rūpa*) and so forth;
that which appears as a sentient being is what manifests as the five sense-faculties within the continuums of oneself and others.
The afflicted mind (*kliṣṭa-manas*) has the appearance of a self,
because it is associated with self-delusion and the other [afflictions].
The six consciousnesses have the appearance of representation (*vijñapti*).
And there is no object for this [consciousness],
because the appearances of objects and sentient beings lack any [corresponding] form,
and the appearances of self and representation are false appearances.
"Because that does not exist, this also does not exist.

Since that fourfold object of apprehension—consisting of form and so forth, the five sense faculties, the mind, and what is termed the six consciousnesses—does not exist, that apprehending consciousness also does not exist.
Therefore, its nature as unreal imagination (*abhūtaparikalpa*) is established.
It is not so, because it does not exist in every respect;
for its existence is not in the manner that the appearance arises,
nor is it non-existent in every respect, because there is the arising of mere illusion.
Why, then, is its non-existence alone not accepted? Because liberation is held to result from its destruction (I.4).
Otherwise, neither bondage nor liberation would be established, and there would be the fault of repudiating both affliction and purification.
[c. The Characteristic of Comprehension] Having thus explained the specific characteristic of unreal imagination (*abhūtaparikalpa*), he now explains its characteristic of comprehension:
how the inclusion of the three natures (*svabhāva*) occurs when there is only unreal imagination.

The imagined, the dependent, and the perfected are taught respectively because of the object, because of the construction of the unreal, and because of the absence of duality. (I.5) The "object" is the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).
Unreal imagination is the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*).
The absence of the grasped and the grasper is the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*). [d. The characteristic of the means for entering the characteristic of non-existence]
Now, he elucidates the characteristic of the means for entering into the characteristic of non-existence within that very unreal imagination:
"Depending upon perception, non-perception arises."
Relying upon non-apprehension, non-apprehension arises.
(I.6) By relying on the apprehension of representation-only, the non-apprehension of objects arises;
by relying on the non-apprehension of objects, the non-apprehension of even representation-only arises.
In this way, one enters into the characteristic of non-existence regarding the apprehended object and the apprehending subject.
Consequently, it is established that the nature of perception is non-perception,
because perception is impossible in the absence of an object to be perceived.

And therefore, one should know the equality of non-apprehension and apprehension. (I.7) Because apprehension is not established as having the nature of apprehension, it is called "apprehension" only because it is a manifestation of unreal objects; thus, even though its true nature is non-apprehension, it is so designated.
[e. *Prabhedalakṣaṇa*]
Now he explains the characteristic of the divisions of that very unreal imagination (abhūtaparikalpa):
"And unreal imagination consists of the mind and mental factors belonging to the three realms," distinguished by their inclusion within the realms of desire, form, and formlessness.
And he explains the characteristic of synonyms:
"In this context, consciousness is the perception of the object, while the mental factors pertain to its specific qualities. (I.8)
In this context, perception of the mere object is consciousness (*vijñāna*);
perception of the specific qualities of the object consists of the mental factors (*caitasika*), such as feeling (*vedanā*) and the rest.
[This is the characteristic of the process of engagement.]
And it explains the characteristic of active engagement:
one is the consciousness as condition, the second is that which pertains to experience.
The mental factors therein consist of experience, discernment, and motivation.
The storehouse-consciousness (ālayavijñāna) is the "condition-consciousness" because it serves as the condition for the other consciousnesses.
The evolving consciousness (pravṛttivijñāna), which functions as experience, is conditioned by that [storehouse-consciousness].
Experience is feeling; discernment is perception;
and the motivators of consciousness are the formative forces, such as volition, attention, and so forth.
[h. Saṃkleśalakṣaṇa] And he explains the characteristic of affliction:
"Because of concealing, because of planting, because of leading, and because of grasping."
The world is afflicted by way of filling, triple discernment, enjoyment, drawing forth, binding, facing toward, and suffering. Among these,
"by way of covering" refers to ignorance, because it obstructs the vision of things as they truly are.
By way of implanting, because the latent impressions of karma are established in consciousness by the formative forces (*saṃskāra*);
by way of leading, because consciousness brings about arrival at the place of rebirth;
and by way of grasping, because the personal existence (*ātmabhāva*) is encompassed by name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).
By means of the six sense bases, there is filling;
by means of contact, there is the threefold discernment;
and by means of feeling, there is enjoyment.
Because of "plowing," craving [acts] upon the renewed existence projected by karma;
because of "binding," grasping [acts] upon consciousness with respect to desires and so forth that are conducive to its arising;
and because of "facing toward," becoming acts by making the karma performed face toward the yielding of its maturation in renewed existence.

The world is afflicted by suffering through birth, aging, and death; this is the threefold and twofold defilement resulting from the sevenfold false conceptualization. (I.11) The threefold defilement is as follows:
There are the affliction of defilement (*kleśa-saṃkleśa*), the affliction of karma (*karma-saṃkleśa*), and the affliction of birth (*janma-saṃkleśa*).
Among these, the affliction of defilement consists of ignorance (*avidyā*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), and grasping (*upādāna*);
the affliction of karma consists of formative forces (*saṃskāra*) and becoming (*bhava*).
The defilement of birth consists of the remaining members;
defilement is twofold:
defilement as cause and defilement as fruit.
In this context, the defilement of cause consists of those members whose intrinsic nature is affliction (*kleśa*) and karma (*karman*); the defilement of fruit consists of the remaining members.
Defilement is sevenfold, corresponding to the seven kinds of causes:
the cause of perversion (*viparyāsa-hetu*).
The projecting cause, the drawing-in cause,
the grasping cause,
and the experiencing cause.
It is the cause of attraction and the cause of agitation;
therein, ignorance is the cause of perversion.
The projecting cause is the formative forces (saṃskāra);
the bringing-to-birth cause is consciousness (vijñāna);
and the appropriating causes are name-and-form (nāmarūpa) and the six sense bases (ṣaḍāyatana).
Contact and sensation are the causes of enjoyment;
craving, grasping, and becoming are the causes of attraction;
birth, aging, and death are the causes of distress.
And all this defilement proceeds from unreal imagination (*abhūtaparikalpa*). Furthermore,
the summary meaning (*piṇḍārtha*) of unreal imagination is elucidated through its ninefold characteristic.
The characteristic of existence,
the characteristic of non-existence, the specific characteristic,
and the characteristic of inclusion.
The characteristic of the means for entering the characteristic of non-existence,
the characteristic of differentiation,
and the characteristic of synonyms.
The characteristic of active engagement and the characteristic of affliction.
[2. Emptiness]
Having thus explained unreal imagination, he now points out how emptiness is to be understood:
"The characteristic, the synonyms, their meaning, the divisions, and the proof—this is to be known as the summary of emptiness. (I.12)
[a. The Characteristic of Emptiness] How is the characteristic to be understood?
For the non-existence of duality, which is the existence of that non-existence, is the characteristic of emptiness.
The non-existence of the duality of the grasped and the grasper,
and the existence of that very non-existence by way of emptiness,
is the characteristic; thus, the fact that emptiness has the characteristic of being the intrinsic nature of non-existence is fully elucidated.
And that which has the nature of the non-existence of those two is neither an entity nor a non-entity.
How is it not an entity? Because it is the non-existence of duality.
How is it not non-existence? Because it is the existence of the absence of duality;
and this is the definition of emptiness.
Therefore, [it exists] as the construction of the unreal.
There is no characteristic of difference or identity.
(I.13) If there were difference, it would not be logical for the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) to be other than the phenomena themselves,
just as [it is not logical for] impermanence or suffering [to be other than the impermanent or suffering things].
If there were identity, there would be no knowledge having purity as its object, nor would there be a universal characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*).
By this, the characteristic that is free from both identity and difference is elucidated.
[b. Synonyms for Emptiness]
How are its synonyms to be understood? In brief, suchness, the limit of reality, the signless, the ultimate truth, and the realm of phenomena are the synonyms of emptiness. (I.14)
[c. The Meaning of the Synonyms for Emptiness] How is the meaning of the synonyms to be understood?
Through non-alteration, non-perversion, the cessation thereof, and the sphere of the noble ones.
And because they are the cause of the noble dharmas, the meanings of the synonyms are as follows in sequence:
it is *tathatā* (suchness) in the sense of being non-otherwise, on account of its being eternally just so;
it is the *bhūtakoṭi* (the limit of reality) in the sense of being non-erroneous, because it is not the object of error.
It is "signless" (*animitta*) in the sense of the cessation of signs, because of the absence of all signs.
It is the "ultimate truth" (*paramārtha*) because it is the objective domain of noble gnosis (*āryajñāna*). It is the object of supreme gnosis.

It is the *dharmadhātu* because it is the cause of the noble qualities (*āryadharma*); for the noble qualities arise with that as their objective support (*ālambana*). For here, the meaning of "element" (*dhātu*) is the meaning of "cause" (*hetu*).
[d. Classification of Emptiness] How is the classification of emptiness to be understood?
It is both afflicted and purified.
Such is its classification.
In what state is it defiled, and in what state is it pure? It is both with stain and without stain.
When it exists together with impurity, it is defiled;
when its impurities have been abandoned, it is pure.
If, having been with impurity, it becomes stainless, how is it that it does not become impermanent due to possessing the nature of change?
Because its purity is held to be like the purification of the water element, gold, and space;
[I.1] it results from the removal of adventitious defilements, but there is no alteration of its intrinsic nature.
[The Sixteenfold Emptiness] This is another classification: the sixteenfold emptiness. Internal emptiness (*adhyātma-śūnyatā*).
emptiness of the external, emptiness of the internal and external, and great emptiness;
The emptiness of emptiness,
the emptiness of the ultimate truth,
and the emptiness of the conditioned.
The emptiness of the unconditioned,
the ultimate emptiness,
and the emptiness of that which has neither beginning nor end.
The emptiness of non-dispersal,
the emptiness of intrinsic nature,
and the emptiness of defining characteristics.
The emptiness of all phenomena,
the emptiness of non-existence,
and the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence.
This very emptiness should be understood in brief as the emptiness of the enjoyer, the enjoyed, their body, and the basis upon which they rest. (Mvbh 25)
And that [emptiness] is the emptiness of that by which, how, and for what purpose it was seen.
(I.171) In this regard, the emptiness of the enjoyer refers to the internal sense bases (*āyatana*), while the emptiness of the enjoyed refers to the external ones.
The "body" of those two—the enjoyer and the enjoyed—is the physical body which serves as their basis;
its emptiness is called "internal emptiness" and "external-internal emptiness.
The "object of support" is the receptacle world (*bhājanaloka*).
Because it is extensive, emptiness is called "great emptiness.
And that by which the internal sense bases and so forth are seen as empty— namely, the knowledge of emptiness—
the emptiness of that [knowledge] is the "emptiness of emptiness."
The emptiness of that which is seen in the form of the ultimate reality is the emptiness of the ultimate (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*);
and the emptiness of that for the sake of which the bodhisattva practices— that for what purpose does he practice?
For the sake of attaining the two kinds of excellence—
the conditioned and the unconditioned that are wholesome—
and for the constant benefit of sentient beings.
For the sake of the ultimate benefit of sentient beings and for the sake of not abandoning cyclic existence:
for if one does not see the emptiness of cyclic existence, which is without beginning or end, one will become weary and abandon cyclic existence.
And for the sake of the inexhaustibility of the wholesome:
that which one neither scatters nor abandons even in the nirvana without remainder— its emptiness is called the "emptiness of non-scattering" (*anavakāra-śūnyatā*).
And for the sake of purifying the lineage (*gotra*);
for the lineage is the fundamental nature (*prakṛti*) because it is innate.
[It is practiced] for the attainment of the primary and secondary marks (*lakṣaṇavyañjana*).

For the sake of attaining the marks of a Great Man together with the secondary characteristics, and for the purification of the Buddha-qualities— such as the powers, the grounds of self-confidence, the unique qualities, and so forth— the Bodhisattva applies himself. I.19
Thus, the establishment of the fourteen types of emptiness should be understood.
What, then, is emptiness here? For emptiness here is the non-existence of the person and of phenomena.
The existence of that non-existence is another emptiness regarding it. (I.20) Emptiness is the non-existence of the person and phenomena,
as well as the existence of that non-existence.
Regarding that aforementioned subject—the enjoyer and so forth—there is another emptiness.
For the purpose of explaining the definition of emptiness, he establishes two kinds of emptiness at the end:
the emptiness of non-existence (*abhāva-śūnyatā*) and the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence (*abhāvasvabhāva-śūnyatā*).

In order to avoid the superimposition of a person (*pudgala*) and phenomena (*dharma*), as well as the denial of their emptiness (*śūnyatā*), the divisions of emptiness should be understood accordingly.
[e. Śūnyatāsādhana]
How is the means of accomplishment to be understood?
If this [nature] were defiled, all embodied beings would never be liberated;
if it were pure, effort would be fruitless. (I.21)

If the emptiness of phenomena were not defiled by adventitious secondary afflictions even when the antidote has not arisen, then all sentient beings would be liberated without effort due to the absence of defilement.
Alternatively, if it were not purified even when the antidote has arisen, then the undertaking for the sake of liberation would be fruitless.
And having established it thus:
it is neither afflicted nor unafflicted, and it is neither pure nor impure.
How is it neither afflicted nor impure?
By its very nature,
because the mind is luminous,
how could it be neither afflicted nor pure?
Because afflictions are adventitious.
(I.22) Thus, the classification of emptiness that was indicated is established.
[Summary of the Meaning of Emptiness]

In this regard, the summary meaning of emptiness should be understood by way of its characteristic and its formal establishment. Therein, it is [to be understood] by way of its characteristic as the characteristic of non-existence and the characteristic of existence.
Furthermore, the characteristic of existence is to be understood through its characteristic of being free from both existence and non-existence,
and through its characteristic of being free from identity and difference.
Moreover, its formal establishment is to be understood through the establishment of its synonyms and so forth.
In this regard, by means of these four modes of teaching, there is the characteristic of emptiness as its own-nature (*svalakṣaṇa*),
its characteristic as activity (*karmalakṣaṇa*), and its characteristic as affliction and purification (*saṃkleśavyavadānalakṣaṇa*).
And the characteristic of reasoning is set forth in the *Madhyāntavibhāga* for the sake of pacifying conceptual construction, fear, indolence,
and doubt.
