(Mvbh 28) With reference to the obscurations (*āvaraṇa*), it is said: [1. The five obscurations, beginning with that which pervades].
The two-fold obscuration is explained as being pervasive, limited, excessive, and that which is abandoned through formal undertaking. Among these,
the pervasive obscuration consists of both afflictive and cognitive obscurations, because it exists in its entirety for those belonging to the lineage of Bodhisattvas.
The afflictive obscuration is partial for those belonging to the lineage of the śrāvakas and others;
it is excessive for those very same individuals who are dominated by conduct such as passion;
and it is equal for those whose conduct is balanced.

The obstruction regarding the taking up and abandoning of *saṃsāra* is the obstruction to non-abiding *nirvāṇa* for those belonging to the lineage of Bodhisattvas; thus, these have been explained as the obstructions for both groups respectively:
those of the Bodhisattva lineage and those of the Śrāvaka and other lineages. [2. The Obstruction of the Nine Bonds of Application]
Furthermore,
the characteristic of the afflictions is ninefold:
the fetters are the hindrances.
The nine fetters are the obscuration of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*).
Of what is this an obscuration?
Of agitation and equanimity,
and because of the non-perception of reality;
the fetter of attachment is an obscuration to spiritual urgency.
The fetter of aversion (*pratigha-saṃyojana*) is to be abandoned through equanimity (*upekṣā*);
for by means of that [fetter], one is unable to remain equanimous even toward an object that is disagreeable.
The remaining [fetters] are obscurations to the vision of reality (*tattvadarśana*).
How so?
For they are, respectively, the object of the view of a self-identity and its basis as well. (II.2)
Regarding the jewels of cessation and the path, as well as gain and honor,
and the thorough understanding of austerity—
the fetters constitute the obstruction.
For the fetter of pride is an obstruction to the full comprehension of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*);
because at the time of clear realization (*abhisamaya*), that [pride] is not abandoned due to the influence of the intermittent or continuous manifestation of the conceit "I am" (*asmimāna*).
The fetter of ignorance is an obstruction to the full comprehension of the objective basis (*vastu*) of the view of a self-identity.
This is because of the lack of full comprehension regarding the aggregates of clinging;
the fetter of views [is abandoned] through the full comprehension of the truth of cessation,
since one is terrified of it by means of the view of a self-identity and the view of grasping at extremes.
And because of the denial [of the truths] through wrong view;
the fetter of clinging (parāmarśa-saṃyojana) [is abandoned] upon the full comprehension of the truth of the path,
because of the clinging to what is otherwise as being supreme and pure.
The fetter of doubt consists in the lack of firm conviction regarding the qualities of the Three Jewels due to a failure to fully understand them;
the fetter of envy consists in the failure to perceive their faults due to a failure to fully understand gain and honor;
and the fetter of avarice consists in the attachment to requisites due to a failure to fully understand ascetic refinement.
[3. Obstructions of the Bodhisattva] [a.
Obstructions regarding the ten virtues, etc.
Furthermore, there are ten types of obstructions regarding the virtuous and so forth. II.3
Furthermore, another obscuration is to be understood as existing with respect to ten kinds of things beginning with the wholesome. What is that obscuration, and what are the wholesome and so forth?
Lack of application, [application] to what is not a proper sphere, and that which is practiced incorrectly;
non-arising, lack of mental attention, and the incompleteness of the accumulations; II.4 the deficiency of the spiritual lineage and the friend, and the exhaustion of the mind.

The deficiency in practice, dwelling among wicked and evil people, the presence of *dauṣṭhulya*, the state of being incomplete with respect to the three [trainings], and the immaturity of wisdom. (II.5)
By their very nature, there is corruption, laziness, and heedlessness;
attachment to existence and to enjoyments, as well as a sunken mind, lack of faith, lack of conviction, and investigation according to the literal expression. II.6–7
Lack of respect for the true Dharma, attachment to gain, as well as laziness, misfortune regarding learning, meagerness [of merit], and lack of cultivation of meditative concentration—
What are the "virtuous" and so forth?
Virtue, enlightenment, undertaking, wisdom, non-delusion, non-obstruction, lack of pride, fearlessness, lack of avarice, and mastery—these are the "virtuous" and so forth. (II.9)
Regarding these [states] such as the wholesome and so forth, he states how many obscurations for each are to be known:
"Indeed, three obscurations are to be known for each of these;
there are three obscurations for the wholesome."
Lack of application, application to what is not a proper sphere, and improper application;
for awakening, these three are: the non-arising of the wholesome, lack of mental attention, and the incompleteness of the accumulations.
The formal undertaking is the generation of the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*).
Its [obstacles] are threefold: deficiency in the spiritual lineage (*gotra*), deficiency in the spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), and a state of mental exhaustion.
Wisdom is the state of being a bodhisattva. Regarding its realization, there are three obscurations: deficiency in practice, dwelling among evil people, and dwelling among wicked people.
In that context, "bad person" refers to a foolish person; "corrupt person" refers to one who is hostile.
Regarding non-delusion, there are three [obstacles]: the depravity of cognitive distortion (*viparyāsa*), [the depravity of afflictions, and the depravity of the knowable].
The state of having any one of the three obstructions— beginning with the afflictions— remaining,
and the immaturity of the wisdom that brings liberation to fruition.
The abandonment of hindrances is non-obstruction;
its three [obstacles] are innate dysfluency,
laziness, and negligence.
There are three types of dedication by which one dedicates the mind elsewhere,
and not toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Attachment to existence, attachment to enjoyments, and a depressed state of mind—
these are the three obstacles to fearlessness. Lack of confidence regarding the person [is the fourth].
Lack of resolve regarding the Dharma;
investigating the meaning according to the literal expression;
and for one who is not stingy, there are three [faults]: lack of respect for the True Dharma.
Respect for gain, honor, and worship, and a lack of compassion toward sentient beings—
these three [obstacles] prevent one from attaining mastery,
because they give rise to karma that leads to the ruin of learning and the ruin of the Dharma.
Limited learning and lack of cultivation of meditative concentration.
[b. The ten causes]
Furthermore, this obscuration regarding the wholesome and so forth should be understood with reference to those objects for which there are ten causes.
There are ten causes:
the cause of arising, such as the eye and so forth, which are the cause of visual consciousness.

The cause of maintenance is, for example, the four nutriments for sentient beings. The cause of support is that which serves as the basis for something else; for example, the receptacle world is the support for the world of sentient beings.
The cause of manifestation;
for example,
light is [the cause] of form.
The cause of transformation is,
for example, fire and so forth with respect to things to be cooked and the like.
The cause of disjunction is, for example, a sickle and so forth with respect to things to be cut and the like.
The cause of transformation (*pariṇatikāraṇa*),
such as goldsmiths and others in the transformation of gold and so forth into the form of bracelets and the like;
and the cause of conviction (*saṃpratyayakāraṇa*).
For example, smoke and so forth are the cause for the cognition of fire and so forth;
likewise, a reason is the cause for a proposition.
The cause of attainment is,
for example, the path and so forth with respect to nirvana and so forth.
In the same way, the obstruction to arising should be understood in relation to the wholesome, because that [wholesome] is something to be produced.

The obstruction to stability pertains to enlightenment, because it is unshakable; the obstruction to steadfastness pertains to the formal undertaking [of the vow], because it serves as the support for the thought of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*);
and the obstruction to manifestation pertains to wisdom, because that must be made manifest.
The obscuration of transformation pertains to non-delusion,
because it is a transformation by way of the overturning of delusion.
The obscuration of separation pertains to non-obscuration, because it is the dissociation from that obscuration.
The obscuration to transformation pertains to inclination, because [inclination] has the characteristic of the transformation of the mind.
The obscuration to conviction pertains to fearlessness,
because one fears due to a lack of conviction.
The obscuration to convincing others exists in regard to non-avarice, because one convinces others through non-avarice regarding the Dharma.
The obscuration to attainment exists in regard to mastery, because that [mastery] is characterized by the attainment of sovereign power (*vibhutva*).
The cause is tenfold with respect to arising, abiding, supporting, and manifesting.
In the cases of modification, separation, understanding, leading across, and attainment.
The eye, food, the earth, a lamp, fire, and so forth are examples of that;
others include a sickle, craftsmanship, smoke, a cause, a path, and the like.
One who desires to attain awakening must first of all generate the roots of virtue;

thereafter, awakening is to be attained through the empowerment of the strength of those roots of virtue. Furthermore, the foundation for the generation of those roots of virtue is the thought of awakening (bodhicitta).
The bodhisattva is the basis for that bodhicitta.
Furthermore, by that bodhisattva who has generated bodhicitta and attained the empowerment of the strength of the roots of virtue, error must be abandoned and non-error must be produced.
Then, when non-error has been established on the path of seeing, all obscurations must be abandoned on the path of cultivation.
Having abandoned all obscurations, one should dedicate all roots of virtue toward unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.
Then, through the empowerment of that power of dedication, one should not be terrified by the teachings of the profound and vast Dharma.
Thus, with an undaunted mind and perceiving the virtues within phenomena, one should extensively proclaim those teachings to others.

Then that Bodhisattva, having thus attained the acquisition of the power of various virtues, quickly realized unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment and attained mastery over all phenomena; such is the sequence for the [cultivation of] the virtuous and so forth.

[4. Obstacles regarding the levels of the factors conducive to enlightenment and the perfections] Furthermore, there is another obstacle regarding the levels of the factors conducive to enlightenment and the perfections.
II.10 [a. Obstacles regarding the factors conducive to enlightenment]

Regarding the factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipakṣya), there are: lack of skill regarding the objective basis, laziness, a twofold deficiency of concentration, non-planting [of roots], weakness, and being corrupted by the depravity of views. II.11
Lack of skill regarding the objects of the foundations of mindfulness is an obscuration; laziness is [an obscuration] to the right efforts;
and the twofold deficiency of concentration is [an obscuration] to the bases of psychic power.

And because of the non-fulfillment of desire, energy, mind, and investigation due to the deficiency of even one of them; and because of the deficiency of the formative forces of abandonment (*prahāṇasaṃskāra*) due to [deficient] cultivation;
there is the failure to plant the factors conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*) within the faculties.
In the *balas*, there is the defect of weakness in those very same faculties due to being interspersed with opposing factors.
In the *bodhyaṅgas*, there is the defect of [wrong] views, because they are brought forth by the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
In the *mārgāṅgas*, there is the defect of *dauṣṭhulya*.
Because they are brought forth by the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), there is an obscuration regarding the perfections (*pāramitā*). This is the obscuration regarding the perfections.

There is an obscuration of sovereignty, of a happy rebirth, and of not abandoning sentient beings; as well as [obscuration] regarding the decrease and increase of faults and virtues, and regarding the introduction [of others]. II.12
Regarding liberation, inexhaustibility, the continuity of the wholesome,
the making [of that] certain, and the enjoyment of the Dharma and its maturation—
II.13 here, among the ten perfections, the obscuration of whichever perfection is indicated by the obscuration of its respective fruit is thus revealed.
In this regard, the obscuration to the perfection of generosity is the obscuration to sovereign power;
the obscuration to the perfection of ethical discipline is the obscuration to a happy rebirth; the obscuration to the perfection of patience is the obscuration to not abandoning sentient beings;
and the obscuration to the perfection of diligence is the obscuration to the decrease of faults and the increase of virtues.
The obscuration regarding the entry of those to be trained is that of the perfection of meditative concentration; the obscuration regarding liberation is that of the perfection of wisdom;
and the obscuration regarding the inexhaustibility of generosity and the other [perfections] is that of the perfection of skillful means.
Because it is rendered inexhaustible through dedication toward enlightenment (*bodhipariṇāmanā*), [there is no obstruction].
For the perfection of aspiration (*praṇidhānapāramitā*), there is the obstruction to the uninterrupted occurrence of wholesome states throughout all births;

for by the power of aspiration, one takes up rebirths favorable to that [wholesome state]. For the perfection of power (*balapāramitā*), there is the obstruction to making that very same wholesome state certain.
Because one is not overcome by opposing factors through the two powers of analytical discernment (*pratisaṃkhyāna*) and cultivation (*bhāvanā*),
the obscuration of the perfection of wisdom (*jñānapāramitā*) is the obscuration regarding the enjoyment of the Dharma and the maturation of oneself and others;
this arises from failing to understand the meaning of what has been heard according to its literal expression.
[c. Obstructions on the Stages] Furthermore, regarding the stages, they are respectively:
the meaning of omnipresence, the meaning of supremacy, and the meaning of the supremacy of natural outflow.
In the sense of being without possession, and in the sense of the non-differentiation of the continuum;
in the sense of being without affliction and without purification, and in the sense of non-diversity. (II.14)
Regarding the meaning of neither less nor more, and as the basis for the fourfold mastery within the dharmadhātu,
this non-afflicted ignorance constitutes a tenfold obscuration;
the ten stages (bhūmis) serve as the antidotes to their respective opposites.

Regarding the tenfold meaning of the dharmadhātu, such as its all-pervasive nature and so forth, that non-afflicted ignorance which exists therein constitutes an obscuration to the ten bodhisattva stages respectively, because it is their antithesis. That is to say, regarding the all-pervasive meaning:
by means of the first stage, one penetrates the all-pervasive meaning of the dharmadhātu.

By means of which one attains the equality of self and others; by the second [perfection], for the sake of the supreme goal, such a thought occurs to him: "Therefore, since the accomplishment is equal, we must apply ourselves to the accomplishment of purification in all its aspects."
By the third [verse], it is for the sake of the excellence of its outflow (*niṣyanda*);

for, having understood the excellence of the hearing of the outflow of the *dharmadhātu*, one would cast oneself even into a fire-pit as large as the triple-thousand great-thousandfold world system for the sake of that [Dharma].
By the fourth, it is for the sake of being without possession (*niṣparigrahatā*); for in this way, even craving for the Dharma (*dharmatṛṣṇā*) is turned away.
On the fifth [ground], for the sake of the non-differentiation of the continuum, [one practices] by means of the ten equalities of the purity of the mental disposition (*cittāśaya*).

On the sixth, for the sake of purification free from defilement, [one practices] because of the penetration that within dependent origination there is no dharma whatsoever that is either defiled or purified.
On the seventh stage, for the sake of non-differentiation, because of being signless (*nirnimitta*), there is no manifestation of the diversity of signs of phenomena such as the sūtras;

on the eighth stage, for the sake of neither decreasing nor increasing, because of the attainment of the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), one does not perceive the decrease or increase of any phenomenon whatsoever, whether in regard to affliction (*saṃkleśa*) or purification (*vyavadāna*).
There are four kinds of mastery: mastery over non-conceptuality, mastery over the purification of the field, mastery over knowledge, and mastery over action.
Among these, one penetrates the state of being the basis for the first two masteries within the *dharmadhātu* by means of the eighth stage alone;
the state of being the basis for mastery over knowledge is attained on the ninth stage through the acquisition of the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*).
The state of being the basis for mastery over karma occurs on the tenth stage, because one performs the welfare of sentient beings through emanations according to one's wish.
Furthermore, in brief:
The obscuration of afflictions and the obscuration of the knowable have been explained;
all obscurations here [are these two], through the destruction of which liberation is sought.
For of this twofold obscuration...
Liberation is held to result from the exhaustion of all obscurations;
this is the summary meaning of the obscurations.
The great obscuration is that which is pervasive; the slight obscuration is that which is localized;
the obscuration of application is that which is excessive.
The obscuration to attainment is that which is equal;
the obscuration to specific attainment is that which pertains to grasping and abandoning;
the obscuration to correct application is the ninefold obscuration of the afflictions.

The obscuration regarding causes is that which pertains to the ten kinds of causal meanings concerning virtue and so forth; the obscuration regarding entry into reality is that which pertains to the factors conducive to enlightenment; the obscuration regarding unsurpassed excellence is that which pertains to the perfections; and the obscuration regarding the attainment of their specific distinctions is that which pertains to the stages.
The obscuration of gathering, in brief, is of two kinds.
The second chapter, on obscurations, in the *Madhyāntavibhāga*.
With reference to reality (*tattva*), it is said:
the reality of the fundamental characteristic and the reality of the characteristic free from error.
The reality consisting of fruit and cause, as well as the subtle and the gross;

that which is established, the object of purification, that which is to be grasped, and the characteristic of differentiation—these are the tenfold realities of skillfulness, serving as the antidote to the view of a self. (III.1–2)
Thus, this tenfold reality consists of: namely, fundamental reality, characteristic reality, non-erroneous reality,
and the reality of cause and fruit.
The reality of the coarse and the subtle,
the well-established reality,
and the reality that is the sphere of purification.
The reality of inclusion, the reality of differentiation, and the reality of skillfulness—
these, moreover, should be understood as tenfold, serving as the antidotes to the tenfold grasping at a self.
Namely: skill in the aggregates,
skill in the elements, skill in the sense bases,
and skill in dependent origination.
Skill in the possible and the impossible, skill in the faculties, skill in the time periods, skill in the truths, skill in the vehicles, and skill in the conditioned and the unconditioned.
[1. Fundamental Reality]
In that regard, the fundamental reality consists of the three natures:
the imagined, the dependent, and the perfected.
In that regard, because of the establishment of reality as something distinct [from the three natures],
what is intended here as "reality" (*tattva*) within these three natures?
(Mvbh 38)
That which is eternally non-existent, that which exists but not in reality, and that which exists and does not exist in reality—these are held to be the three natures (*svabhāva*).

(III.3) The imagined characteristic (*parikalpitalakṣaṇa*) is eternally non-existent; this is the reality (*tattva*) regarding the imagined nature (*parikalpitasvabhāva*), because it is non-erroneous.
The dependent characteristic (paratantra-lakṣaṇa) is both existent and non-existent because it is, in reality, an error; this is the reality within the dependent nature.
The perfected characteristic (pariniṣpanna-lakṣaṇa) is both existence and non-existence in reality; this is the reality within the perfected nature.
[2. The Reality of Characteristics] What is the reality of characteristics?
It is the absence of superimposition and denial regarding phenomena and persons here [in this context].
And the vision of both the apprehended and the apprehender, as well as the vision of existence and non-existence—
when these do not arise through knowledge, that indeed is the characteristic of reality.
When the vision of superimposition and denial regarding the person and phenomena does not arise through one's knowledge, [that is the characteristic of reality].

The characteristic of reality in the imagined nature (parikalpita-svabhāva) is that [the view] of superimposition and denial regarding the grasped and the grasper does not arise through that knowledge. The characteristic of reality in the dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva) is [that same absence of such views].

That in which the view of superimposition and denial regarding existence and non-existence does not arise through knowledge is the characteristic of reality within the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).
This is called the "characteristic of reality" (*lakṣaṇa-tattva*), which is the unerring characteristic within the fundamental reality (*mūla-tattva*).
[3. Non-erroneous Reality (Aviparyāsatattva):

The reality of non-erroneousness consists of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and selflessness, which serve as the antidotes to the errors of permanence and so forth, corresponding respectively to the fundamental reality.
How, then, should impermanence and the other qualities be understood therein?
For the meaning of impermanence is the non-existence [of intrinsic nature], characterized by arising and passing away;
this occurs respectively in the fundamental reality through its states of being with stain and without stain.
(III.5)
For the three natures are the fundamental reality; among them,
the meaning of impermanence is, respectively, the meaning of non-existence.
The meaning of arising and ceasing, and the meaning of being with stain and without stain;
suffering is said to be that which is characterized by grasping, while the other is considered [suffering] by way of connection.

(III.6) In the fundamental reality, suffering is respectively [of two kinds]: first, suffering by way of grasping, because of the grasping of adherence to a person (*pudgala*) and to phenomena (*dharma*).

It should be understood that, within that very fundamental reality (*mūlatattva*), [the nature of suffering] is to be known respectively as being characterized by the three types of suffering (*triduḥkhatā*) in terms of its characteristics (*lakṣaṇataḥ*), and as being connected with suffering in terms of its connection (*saṃbandhataḥ*).
Non-existence (*abhāva*) and the state of not being that (*atadbhāva*), as well as primordial nature (*prakṛti*), are considered emptiness (*śūnyatā*).

Since the imagined characteristic (*parikalpitalakṣaṇa*) does not exist in any manner whatsoever, its emptiness is simply its non-existence. As for the dependent characteristic (*paratantralakṣaṇa*), it does not exist in the way it is imagined, yet it is not non-existent in every respect;
therefore, its emptiness is its state of not being that [imagined form].
Emptiness is the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-lakṣaṇa*), having emptiness as its very essence; thus, its nature is indeed emptiness.
And selflessness is the absence of characteristics (*alakṣaṇa*), which is precisely what is distinct from those [imagined] characteristics. III.7
And its specific characteristic has been explained:
since the imagined nature (parikalpita-svabhāva) lacks even a characteristic, its selflessness is precisely the absence of characteristics (alakṣaṇa).
For the dependent nature (paratantra), a characteristic exists, but not in the manner it is imagined; therefore, its characteristic—being distinct from that [imagined form]—is its selflessness.

The perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), however, is non-self (*nairātmya*) itself; thus, its very nature is non-self. Within the threefold fundamental reality (*mūlatattva*), three kinds of impermanence are elucidated: impermanence in the sense of non-existence (*asadartha-anityatā*), impermanence as arising and ceasing (*utpādabhaṅga-anityatā*), and impermanence as being defiled and purified (*samalanirmala-anityatā*). There are also three kinds of suffering (*duḥkhatā*): the suffering of appropriation (*upādāna-duḥkhatā*), the suffering of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-duḥkhatā*), and the suffering of connection (*saṃbandha-duḥkhatā*).

There are three kinds of emptiness: the emptiness of non-existence (*abhāva-śūnyatā*), the emptiness of not being that [other] nature (*atadbhāva-śūnyatā*), and the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*). There are also three kinds of selflessness: the selflessness of being without characteristics (*alakṣaṇa-nairātmya*), the selflessness of having different characteristics (*vilakṣaṇa-nairātmya*), and the selflessness of having its own characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa-nairātmya*).
[4. The Reality of Cause and Fruit]
The reality consisting of fruit and cause is precisely within that fundamental reality [the three natures], namely the nature of the truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path.
How is it that the threefold fundamental reality constitutes the nature of the truths of suffering and so forth?
Because it possesses the characteristics of impermanence and the rest.
Therefore, the truth of suffering is so considered;
the truth of origination is [so considered] by way of the threefold meaning of origination.
The threefold meaning of origination is as follows:
Furthermore, there are latent predispositions (*vāsanā*), origination (*samutthāna*), and non-separation (*avisaṃyoga*).

(III.8) Latent predispositions as origination refers to the predisposition for adherence to the imagined nature (*parikalpitasvabhāva*). Origination as origination refers to karma and the afflictions (*kleśa*).
Non-separation as origination refers to the same.
It is the non-separation from the obscuration regarding suchness.
The truth of cessation consists of three kinds of cessation;
thus, there are three types of cessation.
The non-arising of the two natures is considered the twofold pacification of stains.

The non-arising of the two natures refers to the non-arising of the grasped and the grasper, while the twofold pacification of stains consists of what is called analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*) and suchness (*tathatā*). Thus, this threefold cessation consists of the cessation of nature and the cessation of duality.
And there is the cessation of intrinsic nature (*prakṛti-nirodha*).
How is the truth of the path (*mārga-satya*) established within the threefold fundamental reality?
It is established in full comprehension (*parijñā*), in abandonment (*prahāṇa*), and in the realization of attainment (*prāpti-sākṣātkṛti*). (III.9)
The truth of the path has been fully explained:
[it consists] in the thorough knowledge of the imagined nature, and in the thorough knowledge and abandonment of the dependent nature.

It should be understood that the establishment of the truth of the path (*mārgasatya*) occurs here through the thorough knowledge (*parijñā*), the abandonment (*prahāṇa*), and the realization (*sākṣātkriyā*) of the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna*).

[5. The Reality of the Gross and the Subtle] Furthermore, regarding the reality of the gross and the subtle, which is the conventional and ultimate truths (*saṃvṛti-paramārtha-satya*), how is it to be understood within the fundamental reality (*mūlatattva*)?
It is "exalted" by way of designation, practice, and likewise by way of manifestation;
for conventional reality is indeed threefold: the conventionality of designation, [the conventionality of practice, and the conventionality of manifestation].
There is the conventionality of practice and the conventionality of manifestation;
by means of these, the status as conventional truth in the fundamental reality should be understood respectively.
But the ultimate [truth] is from one [point of view]. (III.10) Ultimate truth is to be understood as arising from only one, namely, the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).

Furthermore, how is that the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*)? For the ultimate reality is considered to be threefold by way of object, attainment, and practice. Suchness (*tathatā*) is the ultimate as object, because it is the object of the supreme knowledge.

Nirvāṇa is the ultimate reality in terms of attainment (*prāpti-paramārtha*), because it is the supreme goal. The path is the ultimate reality in terms of practice (*pratipatti-paramārtha*), because the supreme goal is its purpose.
How can that which is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and that which is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) [be the ultimate reality]?
The perfected nature is said to be such because of its perfection through being changeless and non-erroneous; thus, the two [other natures] are excluded. III.11
The unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is perfected through the perfection of immutability;

the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), which is subsumed within the truth of the path, is perfected through the perfection of non-perversion, because it is non-perverted with respect to the objects of knowledge (*jñeyavastu*).
[6. Established Reality] How is established reality (prasiddhatattva) established within fundamental reality?
For established reality is of two kinds.
It is both world-renowned and renowned through reasoning. Among these,
that which is world-renowned [is established] from one [of the three natures],
namely, the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).
That object regarding which all worldly people possess a uniformity of perception through a cognition that has entered into conventional familiarity—
such as "this is earth, not fire," or "this is form, not sound," and so forth—
is established by reasoning based on these three [criteria].

That reality which is established for the wise—those who are learned in the meaning of what is logical and are dialecticians—by means of reasoning that establishes proof based upon the three instruments of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); this is the reality that is the sphere of purification.

This reality of the sphere of purification is twofold: the sphere of knowledge that purifies the obscuration of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*), and [the sphere of knowledge that purifies the obscuration of the knowable].

And [the sphere] of the knowledge that purifies the cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇaviśuddhijñānagocara*). This very [sphere of purity] is proclaimed as twofold based on the perfected nature (*pariniṣpannasvabhāva*) alone; for no other nature can be the object of these two types of pure knowledge. (III.12) Indeed, no nature other than the perfected nature serves as the object of the two kinds of purified cognition.
[8. The Reality of Compendium] How is the reality of compendium to be understood within the threefold fundamental reality?
The compendium of the two consists of the sign, the conceptualization, and the name.

Appropriately, with reference to the five entities, there is a subsumption of the sign and conceptualization under the dependent nature (*paratantra*); of the name, under the imagined nature (*parikalpita*);
and of correct knowledge and suchness, they are each subsumed by one alone. (III.13)
Suchness and correct cognition are subsumed within the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).
How is the reality of differentiation (*prabheda-tattva*) to be understood in relation to the fundamental reality (*mūla-tattva*)?
The sevenfold reality of differentiation consists of: the reality of manifestation,
the reality of characteristics,
the reality of representation, and the reality of arrangement.
The reality of false practice,
the reality of purity, and the reality of correct practice. (In this context, there are three kinds beginning with the reality of manifestation.)

Samsara proceeds through beginningless and endless time; because the mind is defiled by suchness, sentient beings are defiled—thus, all the truths of suffering and so forth correspond respectively [to these].
Furthermore, that which is taught as the sevenfold suchness in the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* is as follows: therein, the reality of occurrence (*pravṛtti-tattva*) is twofold.
The fundamental reality should be understood as having the characteristics of the imagined and the dependent,
just as it is with the reality of the mode of occurrence.
The reality of the arrangement and the reality of erroneous practice are likewise each twofold fundamental realities:
one is the reality of characteristics, representation, purity, and correct practice. (III.14)

The four [topics], beginning with the reality of characteristics (*lakṣaṇatattva*), constitute one fundamental reality (*mūlatattva*): the perfected characteristic (*pariniṣpannalakṣaṇa*). [10. Skillfulness in Reality (*kauśalyatattva*)]
It has been stated that the reality of skillfulness serves as the antidote to [wrong] views.
How is it that there are ten kinds of views of a self regarding these aggregates and so forth?
[They consist of viewing the self as] a single cause, an experiencer, an agent, and one who exercises mastery;...
Regarding sovereignty, permanence, the basis of affliction and purification,

as well as being a yogi, and being unliberated or liberated— indeed, it is the view of a self that operates toward these [aggregates and so forth]. This tenfold grasping at a non-existent self proceeds with respect to the aggregates and the rest.
As its antidote, there is tenfold skillfulness, namely: the grasping at unity, the grasping at causality, the grasping at being an enjoyer, the grasping at being an agent,
the grasping at independence, the grasping at sovereignty, and the grasping at permanence.
The grasping at being afflicted or purified, the grasping at being a practitioner,
and the grasping at being unliberated or liberated—
how are these ten kinds of skillful reality included within the fundamental reality?
Since those aggregates and so forth are included within the three natures.
How are they included? "They are included therein by way of the imagined, the conceptualized, and the nature of phenomena. (III.16)
Form is threefold: imagined form is that which is the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) of form;
conceptualized form is that which is the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) of form, for it is therein that the conceptualization of form is performed.
The nature of phenomena (*dharmatārūpa*) is that which is the perfected nature (*pariniṣpannasvabhāva*) of form.
Just as it is with form, so too should the aggregates such as feeling, as well as the elements, sense-fields, and so forth, be applied.

Thus, because the aggregates and other factors are included within the three natures, the tenfold reality of skillfulness (*kauśalyatattva*) should be understood as being contained within the fundamental reality (*mūlatattva*) itself.
It has been stated how skill in the aggregates and so forth serves as the antidote to the ten kinds of views of a self;
however, the meaning of the aggregates and so forth has not yet been explained.
That is now being stated.
(Mvbh 45) [a.
The Meaning of the Aggregates] First, the meaning of the aggregates is [to be understood in terms of] multiplicity, condensation, and delimitation.
First of all, those aggregates (skandhas) are to be understood by way of three meanings:
by the meaning of multiplicity, as in the detailed explanation "whatever form there is, whether past, future, or present";
and by the meaning of condensation, as in "having condensed all that into a single unity."

Furthermore, because the characteristics of form and so forth are established as distinct by way of delimitation, the meaning of "aggregate" (*skandha*) is indeed the meaning of "heap" (*rāśi*); for in the world, the meaning of "heap" is observed in this very sense.
[b. The Meaning of Element (*dhātu*)]
And another meaning is considered to be that of the seeds of the grasper, the grasped, and the grasping thereof.
(III.17) What is this other [meaning], the realm (*dhātu*)? In that context, the meaning of the seeds of the grasper refers to the eye-realm (*cakṣurdhātu*) and so forth;
the meaning of the seeds of the grasped refers to the form-realm (*rūpadhātu*) and so forth.

The meaning of those as the seeds of grasping refers to the eye-consciousness element and so forth. Furthermore, the meaning of the sense bases (*āyatana*) is from the perspective of being the gateways for the arising of feeling, the discernment of objects, and enjoyment.
What else is the sense-field (*āyatana*)?
In that regard, there are six internal sense-fields in the sense of being the doors for the arising of the experience of feeling;
and there are six external [sense-fields] in the sense of being the doors for the arising of the experience of the discernment of objects.
[d. The Meaning of Dependent Origination] The meaning of dependent origination is, furthermore, the absence of superimposition and denial regarding cause, fruit, and effort. III.18

The meaning of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) is the sense of neither superimposing nor denying causes, fruits, and activities. In this context, "superimposition of the cause" refers to the conceptualization of discordant causes for the formative forces (*saṃskāra*) and so forth. "Denial of the cause" refers to the conceptualization that they are causeless. "Superimposition of the fruit" refers to the conceptualization that the formative forces and so forth, which possess a self-nature, proceed by means of conditions such as ignorance.

The denial of the result (*phalāpavāda*) consists in the conceptualization that the formative forces (*saṃskāra*) and so forth do not exist as conditions such as ignorance (*avidyā*). The superimposition of activity (*kriyāsamāropa*) consists in the conceptualization of an operation by ignorance and so forth in the production of the formative forces and so forth. The denial of activity (*kriyāpavāda*) consists in the conceptualization of inefficacy. Due to the absence of these two, one should understand non-superimposition and non-denial (*asamāropānapavāda*). [This is the meaning of *sthāna* and *asthāna*.]

The other [subject], namely the possible and the impossible (*sthānāsthāna*), should be understood in the sense of sevenfold dependence (*pāratantrya*): regarding the undesirable, the desirable, and the pure; regarding simultaneous arising and sovereignty; and regarding attainment and manifestation. (III.19)

In that regard, there is dependence regarding the undesirable, because one goes to an evil rebirth through misconduct even against one’s will; there is dependence regarding the desirable, because one goes to a happy rebirth through good conduct. There is dependence regarding purification, because one does not bring an end to suffering without abandoning the five hindrances and without cultivating the seven factors of enlightenment. And there is dependence regarding simultaneous arising, because two Tathāgatas do not appear at the same time, neither before nor after the other.

Furthermore, regarding sovereignty, there is dependence on another because two universal monarchs do not arise simultaneously in a single world-system; regarding attainment, there is dependence on another because a woman cannot become a universal monarch and so forth;

regarding manifestation, there is dependence on another because a woman does not realize the enlightenment of a Pratyekabuddha or unsurpassed enlightenment, whereas for one endowed with right view there is dependence on another because they do not manifest acts such as killing, while for an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) such acts do manifest, and so forth in detail.
This should be understood in accordance with the *Bahudhātuka-sūtra*.
Furthermore, the faculties (*indriya*) are of twenty-two kinds.
By way of grasping, abiding, connecting, experiencing, and the two kinds of purification;

from the sense of grasping up to the sense of the two kinds of purification, these [faculties] exercise sovereignty over them. For the six [faculties], beginning with the eye, exercise sovereignty in the grasping of objects such as visible form; the life-faculty exercises sovereignty in abiding, because by its sovereignty there is no death.

In the continuity of the family, the faculties of female and male predominate because they bring about the birth of offspring; in enjoyment, the feeling faculties [predominate] because of the enjoyment of the fruits of wholesome and unwholesome karma;
in mundane purification, faith and the others [predominate]; and in supramundane purification, the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" and the others [predominate].
[III.20] Regarding the meaning of the time periods (*adhvārtha*):

"Likewise, another [time period] is [defined] by the sense of the utilization or non-utilization of fruit and cause. What is this other? It is the three time periods. According to their respective application: the past time period is defined by the sense of having utilized the fruit and cause; the future time period is defined by the sense of not yet having utilized the fruit and cause; and the present time period is defined by the sense of utilizing the cause while not yet having utilized the fruit.
It should be understood as follows:
[h. The Meaning of the Four Truths] by way of sensation, its cause, its object, and the engagement with that cause.
Another [set] is intended because it serves as the antidote to that [craving].
(III.21) What is this other? It is the four truths.

Among them, the truth of suffering is understood in the sense of feeling together with its cause, based on the principle that "whatever is felt here is suffering. Furthermore, the cause of feeling should be understood as those phenomena that serve as the basis for feeling.
The truth of origination is understood through the practice directed toward its cause; that is, the practice which has the truth of suffering as its objective.
The truth of cessation is understood in the sense of the pacification of those two;
the truth of the path is understood in the sense of being the antidote.
[1. The Meaning of the Three Vehicles:
Through knowledge that is free from conceptualization regarding virtues and faults, and by means of departure—either through another or by oneself—the other [aspects] are to be known.
The three vehicles are applied accordingly;
therein, through the knowledge of the virtues and faults of nirvāṇa and saṃsāra, [one relies] on others.

The Śrāvakayāna is to be understood as that which leads to deliverance through hearing [the teachings] from others; the Pratyekabuddhayāna as that which leads to deliverance by oneself without having heard [them] from others;
and the Mahāyāna as that which leads to deliverance by oneself through non-conceptual knowledge.
From the perspective of conceptual designation and its cause, from the perspective of signs, and from the perspective of tranquility and its object, the last [category] has been proclaimed. III.22

Therein, the conditioned and the unconditioned consist of: (1) the designation, which refers to the group of names and so forth; (2) the cause, which is the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) comprised of seeds;
(3) the sign, which is comprised of the environment, the body, and objects of enjoyment;
and (4) that which is comprised of the evolving consciousnesses, namely, the mind (*manas*), apprehension (*udgraha*), and conceptualization (*vikalpa*).
This sign, together with its conceptual designations, its causes, and its associated mental factors, should be understood as conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
Among these, the mind (*manas*) is that which has the constant mode of activity of cogitation;
apprehension (*udgraha*) refers to the five groups of sensory consciousness; and conceptualization (*vikalpa*) is the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
Because that [conceptualization] is discursive, the unconditioned is, moreover, tranquility and cessation.

Suchness is the object of tranquility; for it is tranquility, cessation, and the path—considering both that which is tranquility and that by which there is tranquility—as the "object of tranquility. Thus, suchness is the object of tranquility because suchness is the objective support of the path.
Because the path is characterized by tranquility, and because one attains tranquility through it;
in this sense, knowledge regarding the aggregates and so forth should be understood as skill in the aggregates and so forth.
[Tattvapiṇḍārtha]
This is the summary meaning of reality (*tattva*).
In brief, reality is twofold: the reality of the mirror (*ādarśatattva*) and...

The reality of the object of vision (*dṛśyatattva*) therein is the mirror-like reality (*ādarśatattva*), which is the fundamental reality (*mūlatattva*), because the remaining [realities] are seen therein.

The reality of the object of vision is ninefold: the reality of the object of vision free from conceit (*nirabhimāna-dṛśyatattva*) and the reality of the object of vision free from error (*aviparyāsa-dṛśyatattva*).
The reality of the objects perceived in the departure via the Śrāvaka vehicle, and the reality of the objects perceived in the departure via the Mahāyāna;
[this is] because of maturing [beings] through the coarse [method].
The reality of the object perceived in the refutation of opponents is due to liberation through subtle [analysis],
because one refutes them through reasoning based on examples. The reality of the object perceived in the illumination of the Mahāyāna is [due to the same].

The reality of what is seen as the entry into all aspects of the knowable; the reality of what is seen as the illumination of suchness that is non-erroneous; and the reality of what is seen as the entry into all intentional meanings regarding the basis for the grasping of a self. // 8 //
The third chapter, on Reality, in the Madhyāntavibhāga-śāstra.
The cultivation of the antidotes, which is the cultivation of the factors conducive to enlightenment, must now be explained. [A.
The Four Foundations of Mindfulness]
In that regard, first of all:

"The cultivation of the applications of mindfulness is for the sake of entering the four truths, by way of [their] corruption, being the cause of thirst, being substantial entities, and non-delusion. (IV.1)
For corruption is manifested through the body;
by examining that, one enters into the truth of suffering,
because its characteristic is that of conditioned phenomena accompanied by corruption.
For corruption (*dauṣṭhulya*) is the suffering inherent in conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*). Because of this, the Noble Ones perceive every contaminated thing as suffering.
Feeling (*vedanā*) is the cause of craving; by examining it, one enters into the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*).
The mind is the objective basis for the adherence to a self; by examining it, one enters the truth of cessation because the fear of the annihilation of the self has been removed.
By examining phenomena (*dharma*), one enters the truth of the path through the absence of delusion regarding phenomena that are defiled or purified. Therefore...
First, the cultivation of the foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) is established for the sake of entering the Four Noble Truths.
Following that is the cultivation of the right efforts (samyakprahāṇa), because:

When the discordant factors and their antidotes have been thoroughly understood in every respect, the vigor for their removal and attainment proceeds in four ways. (IV.2) Through the cultivation of the applications of mindfulness, once the discordant factors and the antidotes are fully known in all their modes, vigor proceeds in four ways for the sake of the departure of the discordant factors and the attainment of the antidotes.
"For the abandoning of evil, unwholesome states that have arisen," and so forth.
(Mvbh 51) [c.
The Four Bases of Psychic Power]
The pliability of stability therein for the fulfillment of all goals follows from the cultivation of the eight formative forces (*saṃskāra*) through the abandonment of the five faults.
In that cultivation of vigor for the removal of those [faults], there is the stability of the mind.

Workability consists of the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*), because they are the cause for the accomplishment of all goals. Here, "stability" should be understood as the stability of the mind, which is meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Therefore, the bases of psychic power follow immediately after the right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*).
Furthermore, that workability should be understood as resulting from the cultivation of the eight formative forces of abandonment (*prahāṇasaṃskāra*) in order to eliminate the five faults.
[The Five Faults: What are the five faults? He says:
laziness, forgetting the instruction, lethargy, and agitation.
Non-application and application—these are considered the five faults.
Among them, lethargy and excitement are treated as a single fault;
lack of application at the time of pacifying lethargy and excitement is a fault.
Regarding the formative effort for tranquility:
how are the eight formative forces of abandonment established for the sake of abandoning these?
[The Eight Formative Forces of Abandonment] How are the eight formative forces of abandonment established for their abandonment?

There are four factors for the abandonment of laziness: zeal, exertion, faith, and pliancy; these, moreover, should be understood in their respective order as the basis, that which is based upon it, its cause, and its fruit. Zeal is the basis of exertion.

Exertion (*vyāyāma*) is dependent upon its basis, which is zeal (*chanda*); faith (*śraddhā*) is the cause of that zeal, because when there is conviction (*saṃpratyaya*), there arises a longing [for the goal]. The fruit of that exertion which is dependent [upon zeal] is pliancy (*prasrabdhi*), due to the attainment of a specific state of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) by one who has initiated vigor (*vīrya*).

The remaining four formative forces of abandonment (*prahāṇasaṃskāra*)—namely, mindfulness (*smṛti*), clear comprehension (*saṃprajanya*), volition (*cetanā*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*)—are the respective antidotes to the four faults. Furthermore, these factors beginning with mindfulness should be understood in their proper sequence.

Non-forgetfulness regarding the object, the recognition of laxity and excitement, the formative activity for their removal, and smooth flow in tranquility. (IV.5) Mindfulness is non-forgetfulness regarding the object; clear comprehension is the recognition of laxity and excitement when there is non-forgetfulness through mindfulness.
Volition (*cetanā*) is the formative effort made after having understood [the state of mind] in order to eliminate that [laxity and excitement].
When that laxity and excitement have been stilled, equanimity (*upekṣā*) is the mind’s state of flowing smoothly and effortlessly.
[d. The Five Faculties]

Immediately after the bases of psychic power (ṛddhipāda) come the five faculties (indriya), beginning with faith. How are they established? When the factors conducive to liberation (mokṣabhāgīya) have been planted, [the faculties are established] through the predominance of aspiration and application, as well as through non-forgetfulness, non-distraction, and investigation regarding the object of focus. (IV.6)
The term "by way of predominance" carries over.

When the roots of merit conducive to liberation have been planted in a mind made pliant by the bases of psychic power, there is [predominance] through the predominance of desire, the predominance of application,
and the predominance of non-forgetfulness regarding the object.
The five faculties, beginning with faith, are to be understood respectively as having non-diffusion as their predominance and discernment as their predominance.
[e. The Five Powers] Those very same qualities beginning with faith, when they have become powerful, are called the powers (*balāni*).
Furthermore, their state of being powerful is as follows:
For it is through the refinement of the opposing factors that,
when those [wholesome states] are no longer intermingled with their opposites such as lack of faith and so forth, [they become purified].
Why is there this sequential explanation of faith and the others? Because each subsequent one is the fruit of the preceding one;
for it is one who has faith in cause and effect that exerts vigor.
For one who has initiated vigor, mindfulness becomes established;
for one whose mindfulness is established, the mind becomes concentrated;
and with a concentrated mind, one understands things as they truly are.

The faculties (*indriya*) of one who has planted the roots conducive to liberation have been explained. Now, as for the factors conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*), should they be understood as being in the stage of the faculties or in the stage of the powers (*bala*)? Two by two, the factors conducive to penetration are both faculties and powers. Heat (*uṣmagata*) and the Summits (*mūrdhan*) are the faculties.
The patiences and the supreme mundane dharmas are the powers.
Immediately after the powers are the factors of enlightenment; how are they established?
The limb of basis, the limb of intrinsic nature, the third is the limb of departure,

the fourth is the limb of benefit, and the limb free from affliction is considered to be threefold. (IV.8) On the path of seeing, the limbs of enlightenment are the factors of awakening (*bodhyaṅga*).
In that context, mindfulness is the limb that serves as the basis for awakening;
the investigation of phenomena is the limb that constitutes its intrinsic nature;
and vigor is the limb of departure.
The factor of benefit is joy (*prīti*).
The factors of non-affliction (*asaṃkleśa*) are threefold: pliancy (*prasrabdhi*), concentration (*samādhi*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*).
For what purpose, then, are the factors of non-affliction taught as being threefold?
(Mvbh 54) Here, it is taught by way of cause, basis, and intrinsic nature.
The cause of non-affliction is pliancy, because [the opposite] is the cause of affliction due to its being the cause of *dauṣṭhulya*.
And because it is the antidote to that, its basis is meditative concentration;
its intrinsic nature is equanimity.
[The Eight Limbs of the Path]

Following the factors of enlightenment (bodhyaṅga) are the factors of the path (mārgāṅga). How are they established? They consist of: discernment, attainment, the threefold confidence of others, and the antidote to opposing factors; thus, the factors of the path are eightfold. [IV.9]

On the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*)— both mundane and supramundane, obtained subsequent to [realization]— is the limb for discerning it, by which one discerns one's own attainment.
Right intention (*samyaksaṃkalpa*) and right speech (*samyagvāk*) are the limbs for causing others to attain it,
because one causes that attainment through speech accompanied by its origination.
The factors for inspiring confidence in others are threefold: right speech, right action, and right livelihood;
for by means of these, in that order, one is held in high esteem by others regarding one's view, ethical conduct, and austerity.
Through right speech, by means of discourse, conversation, and definitive resolution, one inspires confidence in others regarding one’s wisdom.

Right action consists in not performing what should not be done regarding ethical discipline; right livelihood consists in seeking robes and so forth through the Dharma, with moderation, and with austerity.
The factors that serve as antidotes to the opposing elements are likewise threefold: right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration; for these function, respectively, as follows:

The state of being the counteragent to the afflictions (*kleśa*), the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), and the obstacles to mastery (*vaibhutvavipakṣa*). For the obstacle is threefold: the affliction to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanāheya*), and the secondary affliction consisting of lethargy and excitement (*layauddhatya*).
And the obstacle to mastery is the hindrance to the production of the specific qualities; therein, right effort is the antidote to the first, because through it there is the cultivation of the path.
Right mindfulness is the antidote to the second, because when mindfulness is well-established regarding the signs of calm abiding and so forth, there is an absence of lethargy and excitement.
Right concentration is the antidote to the third, because by relying on meditative absorption, one produces qualities such as the superknowledges.
[h. The Classification of the Cultivation of the Antidote] This cultivation of the antidote should be understood briefly as threefold:
favorable, inverted, and accompanied by continuity; and its opposite. IV.11
And there is cultivation that is non-erroneous yet accompanied by error;

[cultivation] that is erroneous but conducive to non-error; [cultivation] that is non-erroneous yet accompanied by error; and [cultivation] that is non-erroneous and unaccompanied by error, respectively in the stages of ordinary beings, those in training, and those beyond training.
However, for Bodhisattvas...
Its distinction [from that of the Śrāvakas] arises from its object, mental attention, and attainment.

(IV.12) For the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, the object is the body and so forth belonging to their own continuum; for Bodhisattvas, it is those belonging to both their own and others' continua. The Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas attend to the body and so forth through aspects such as impermanence.
Bodhisattvas, however, do so through the yoga of non-apprehension.
Śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas cultivate the applications of mindfulness and so forth only for the sake of dissociation from the body and other aggregates;
bodhisattvas do not [cultivate them] for the sake of dissociation.
It is not for the sake of non-separation;
rather, it is solely for the sake of non-abiding nirvana.
Thus has been explained the cultivation of the antidotes.
(Mvbh 56) [2. Therein,
the States] What therein are the states?

It is designated as the stage of the cause, the entry, the application, and the fruit; it is distinguished by what is to be done and what is not to be done; and it is both with further stages and without further stages. IV.13
In terms of resolute belief, entry, departure, prophecy, teaching,
consecration, attainment, and the praise of benefits,
the performance of duties has been indicated. IV.1a-b.

In this context, the causal stage is that of a person established in the lineage; the stage of entry is that of one who has generated the thought of awakening; the stage of application is from the generation of the thought of awakening onwards until the fruit is attained;
the stage of fruition is when it has been attained;
and the stage of having further tasks to perform is that of one in training (śaikṣa).
The state of having nothing further to be done belongs to one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
The state of excellence belongs to one endowed with special qualities such as the superknowledges (*abhijñā*) and so forth.
The superior state belongs to a bodhisattva who has entered the stages, surpassing those such as the śrāvakas.

The state of the Buddha is the unsurpassed state, because there is no further state beyond it. The state of resolute belief (*adhimukti*) belongs to Bodhisattvas throughout the entire stage of practice through resolute belief (*adhimukticaryābhūmi*). The state of entry is on the first stage (*bhūmi*); the state of departure is on the six stages following that;
the state of prophecy (*vyākaraṇa*) is on the eighth stage; the state of being a teacher (*kathikatva*) is on the ninth; and the state of consecration (*abhiṣeka*) is on the tenth.
The state of attainment is the *dharmakāya* of the Buddhas;
the state of benefit is the *sāmbhogikakāya*;
and the state of performing activities is the *nirmāṇakāya*.

All these various states, when summarized, should be understood as threefold within the *dharmadhātu*: impure, both impure and pure, and completely pure, according to their respective natures. (IV.15)
In this context, the impure state is defined from the causal stage up to the stage of application; the impure-pure state belongs to those in training (*śaikṣa*);
and the completely pure state belongs to those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
Therefore, the formal classification of persons (*pudgala*) is considered to be established according to these correspondences.

Therefore, based on these distinctions of stages, the classification of individuals (pudgala) should be understood as appropriate— such as "this one abides in the lineage" (gotrastha), "this one has entered" (avatīrṇa), and so forth.
The explanation of the stages is concluded.
[3. Attainment of the Fruit] What is the attainment of the fruit?
It is the state of being a vessel, known as maturation (*vipāka*), by virtue of its power and predominance. IV.16
Delight, increase, and purity are the results in their respective order:
delight is the maturation that is conducive to the wholesome and makes one a fit vessel;
increase is the preeminence of the wholesome resulting from the sovereignty of being a fit vessel.
Inclination is that which, through prior practice, is an inclination toward the wholesome;
increase is the nourishment of the roots of the wholesome through the practice of wholesome dharmas in the present;
and purification is the abandonment of obscurations.
These five kinds of results should be understood in their respective order:

the ripened result (*vipākaphala*), the dominant result (*adhipatiphala*), the outflow result (*niṣyandaphala*), the result of human effort (*puruṣakāraphala*), and the result of dissociation (*visaṃyogaphala*).
[They correspond respectively to] the subsequent, the first, from the practice thereof, and from the completion. (IV.17)
"In brief, the other fruit [is distinguished] by way of conformity, by way of the opposite, by way of dissociation, by way of excellence, and by way of being higher or unsurpassed.

(IV.18) It should be understood that the successively higher fruits— beginning with the arising of the thought of enlightenment from the spiritual lineage (gotra)— are to be known through this sequence."
The initial fruit is the first acquisition of supramundane dharmas; the fruit of practice is that which follows thereafter during the stage of one-in-training (śaikṣa);
and the fruit of completion consists of the dharmas of one beyond training (aśaikṣa).
The fruit of conformity should be understood as the successive fruits by way of being the proximate cause (*upaniṣad*).
The fruit of the adverse side is the path of abandonment (*prahāṇamārga*), which is precisely the initial fruit;
it is the counteragent (*pratipakṣa*) that is intended.

The fruit of dissociation is the realization of cessation; it is both the fruit of practice and the fruit of completion, consisting in the dissociation from the afflictions of those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), respectively.
The fruit of distinction consists in the specific qualities such as the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).
The higher fruit consists of the bodhisattva stages because they are superior to other vehicles; the unsurpassed fruit is the Buddha stage.
These four are merely distinctions within the fruit of the completion of cultivation; this other fruit is described briefly here, but in detail it is immeasurable.
[Summary of the Cultivation of Antidotes]
In this regard, the summary meaning of the cultivation of the counteragent is as follows:
the cultivation of thorough understanding, the cultivation of abrasion, the cultivation of preparation,
and the cultivation of further undertaking.
Connected cultivation (*śliṣṭabhāvanā*) is so called because of its connection with the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).

There is also cultivation that has entered (*praviṣṭabhāvanā*), superior cultivation (*utkṛṣṭabhāvanā*), initial cultivation (*ādibhāvanā*), middle cultivation (*madhyabhāvanā*), and final cultivation (*paryavasānabhāvanā*).

Furthermore, there is cultivation with something higher (*sottarā bhāvanā*) and unsurpassed cultivation (*niruttarā bhāvanā*), which is distinguished by its object (*ālambana*), mental attention (*manaskāra*), and attainment (*prāpti*).
The summary meaning of the states is as follows:
the state of potentiality belongs to one established in the lineage;
the state of undertaking extends up to the stage of application.
The impure state, the impure-pure state, the pure state,
the state with ornaments,
and the state of pervasion, due to its pervading the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).
And the state of unsurpassedness.
The summary meaning of the fruits is presented by way of their synthesis, their specific distinctions, previous practice, successive accomplishment,
and by way of brief statement and detailed exposition.
Among these, [the first is] by way of synthesis:
There are five fruits;
the remaining ones are distinguished by those.
By virtue of previous practice, there is the fruit of maturation (vipākaphala).
The other four are by way of successive accomplishment;
four beginning with the "result of the subsequent" are from the perspective of the summary, while six beginning with the "conformable result" are from the perspective of the detailed explanation.
