The supreme [perfection] consists of twelve aspects:
V.2 magnificence, extensiveness, dedication, and the nature of inexhaustibility.
Uninterruptedness, lack of difficulty, wealth, and possession;
the undertaking, attainment, outflow, and perfection—these are considered the supreme [perfections].
Thus, this supreme [perfection] is considered to be of twelve kinds.
Namely: the supremacy of magnanimity, the supremacy of extensiveness, the supremacy of purpose, the supremacy of inexhaustibility, the supremacy of continuity,
the supremacy of ease, the supremacy of wealth,
the supremacy of appropriation, the supremacy of undertaking, the supremacy of attainment, the supremacy of outflow, and the supremacy of perfection.
In this context, the supremacy of magnanimity (*audārya*) is to be understood through the lack of desire for any worldly prosperity and through its excellence.
The supremacy of duration (*āyatattva*) is due to cultivation over three incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*).
The supremacy of purpose (*adhikāra*) is due to the commitment to performing what is beneficial for all sentient beings.

The supremacy of inexhaustibility [is attained] because, through the dedication toward great enlightenment (*mahābodhi*), there is no ultimate exhaustion. The supremacy of continuity [is attained] because, through the resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*) in the equality of self and others, one fulfills the perfections (*pāramitā*) by means of giving and so forth for the sake of all sentient beings. The supremacy of ease [is attained] because, by merely rejoicing (*anumodanā*), one fulfills the perfections of others' giving and so forth. [This is] the supremacy of wealth.
The supremacy of appropriation consists in the fulfillment of generosity and the other perfections through such means as the Gaganagañja-samādhi, because they are embraced by non-conceptual gnosis.

The supremacy of undertaking occurs on the stage of practice through resolute belief (*adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*) at the level of superior patience; the supremacy of attainment occurs on the first bhūmi; and there is the supremacy of natural outflow (*niṣyanda*).
In the other eight stages,
it is the supremacy of accomplishment; in the tenth stage and in the state of a Tathāgata,
it is through the accomplishment of a Bodhisattva and the accomplishment of a Buddha.
And therefore, in the ultimate sense, the ten perfections are so considered,
because this twelvefold supremacy is found within them;
thus they are supreme.
For this reason, there are ten perfections (*pāramitā*).
To explain their names for some who ask, "Which ten? it is said:
generosity, ethical discipline, patience, vigor, meditative concentration, wisdom, and skillful means;
Vow, power, and knowledge—these are the ten perfections.
What is the function of each of them?
Their functions are: favoring others, non-obstruction, and the endurance of that [obstruction].
Virtue, increase, capacity, descent and liberation,
inexhaustibility, constant activity, and the certain ripening of enjoyments—
these, respectively, are their functions. (V.6)
For by means of generosity, the bodhisattva benefits sentient beings;
by means of ethical discipline, he does no harm to others;
and by means of patience, he endures the harm inflicted by others.
Through vigor, one increases virtues;
through meditative concentration, one wins them over and causes them to enter by means of supernatural powers and so forth;
and through wisdom, one liberates them by providing correct instruction.

Through the perfection of skill in means (*upāyakauśalyapāramitā*), by dedicating [the roots of virtue] toward great awakening (*mahābodhi*), one makes generosity and the other perfections inexhaustible.

Through the perfection of aspiration (*praṇidhānapāramitā*), by securing rebirths favorable [to practice], one always engages in generosity and the others by encountering the arising of Buddhas in all births. Through the perfection of power (*balapāramitā*), by means of the two powers of analytical reflection (*pratisaṃkhyāna*) and cultivation (*bhāvanā*), one engages in generosity and the others with certainty.
Because it is not overcome by opposing factors,

through the perfection of wisdom, one removes delusion regarding phenomena as they are expressed in words, experiences the enjoyment of the teachings that have generosity and the other perfections as their dominant influence,
and brings sentient beings to maturity.
The supreme practice has been explained.
[b. Practice of Mental Attention] (Mvbh 63)
What is the practice of mental attention?
It is the mental engagement with the Mahāyāna Dharma according to how it has been taught, by means of the Bodhisattva’s threefold wisdom at all times. V.7

Regarding generosity and the other perfections, the practice of mental application consists of the frequent mental engagement with the dharmas—such as the sūtras—as they have been taught in the Mahāyāna, by means of the wisdom consisting of hearing, reflection, and cultivation.
What benefit does this mental application by means of the threefold wisdom produce?
It serves for the nourishment of the element, for entry [into reality], and for the accomplishment of the goal.

For one who attends to the mind through wisdom consisting of hearing, there is nourishment of the constituent elements (*dhātu*). Through wisdom consisting of reflection, one enters into the meaning of that which was heard with a state of being.
Through wisdom consisting of cultivation, one attains the accomplishment of the goal by means of purifying the entry into the stages (*bhūmi*).

Furthermore, that practice of mental attention should be known as being conjoined with the ten practices of the Dharma (*dharmacarita*). It should be understood as being embraced by these ten practices of the Dharma. What are the ten forms of the practice of the Dharma?
Writing, worshiping, giving, listening,

reciting, memorizing, explaining, self-study, reflecting, and meditating— these are [the practices] regarding that Mahāyāna. (V.9) Writing the Mahāyāna, worshiping it, giving it to others, and listening to it as it is being recited by another;
And it consists of reciting it oneself, memorizing it, teaching it to others, and personally studying its words or its meaning.
Reflection and cultivation—
this tenfold practice indeed constitutes an immeasurable mass of merit.
Why is it that in the sūtras the practice of the Dharma is taught as having exceedingly great fruit only in the Mahāyāna, and not in the Śrāvakayāna?
It is for two reasons:
because of its superiority and because of its inexhaustibility.
How is it by way of distinction?
How is it by way of inexhaustibility? It is through the assistance of others and through non-cessation. // V.10 //
Its excellence is due to its activity of benefiting others;
its inexhaustibility should be understood as being because it does not cease even in parinirvāṇa, owing to its lack of final rest.
The practice of mental attention has been explained.
What is the practice in accordance with the Dharma (*anudharmapratipatti*)?
Undistracted and transformed by non-perversion is that which conforms to the Dharma;
thus, this practice in accordance with the Dharma is twofold:
namely, the undistracted and that which is transformed by non-perversion.
[Transformed by non-distraction: In that regard, it is undistracted because of the absence of the six kinds of distraction.
Therein, the six kinds of distraction are as follows:
Natural distraction,
external distraction,
internal distraction, distraction of signs, distraction of depravity, and distraction of mental attention.
"What are the characteristics by which this [state] is to be known? To this he says:
V.11 Arising, attachment to objects, likewise relishing, lethargy, and agitation; conceit regarding one's attainments, and even the sense of "I" in mental attention.
(65) "And a lowly mind as well as distraction should be thoroughly understood by the wise.
(V.12) Thus, these six kinds of distraction characterized in this way are what must be thoroughly understood by a bodhisattva.

In that context, emergence from meditative concentration occurs through the five groups of sensory consciousnesses. Natural distraction is the wandering toward objects; external distraction is the outward diffusion [of the mind].
Internal distraction consists of the relishing of meditative concentration, as well as lethargy and agitation. Distraction of signs is the underlying intention for self-aggrandizement.
Having made that the sign, due to its application,
there is mental attention accompanied by ego-grasping; this is the distraction of *dauṣṭhulya*, because the manifestation of the conceit "I am" occurs through the power of *dauṣṭhulya*.
A lowly state of mind;
distraction of mental attention due to the active engagement of the mental attention of the Lesser Vehicle.
[The Transformation Free from Error]

In this regard, non-perversion should be understood with respect to ten kinds of entities, namely: the letter, the meaning, mental attention, non-dispersal, the two characteristics, impurity and purity, adventitiousness, and being neither terrified nor conceited. V.13
In that regard:

"Due to conjunction and indeed due to familiarity, and also due to disjunction and non-familiarity, there is the existence and non-existence of the object; this is the absence of error concerning the phoneme. (V.14)

When there is a conjunction of phonemes, because they are uttered without interruption, one becomes familiar with them such that "this is the name of this [object]," whereby they possess meaning; conversely, through the opposite, they are meaningless.
That which is the vision of it in this way should be understood as non-perversion regarding the phoneme.
How is there non-perversion regarding the object?
There is appearance as a duality and likewise non-existence; this is non-perversion regarding the object, being devoid of both existence and non-existence.
(V.15) It appears as a duality—that is, as the grasped and the grasper—because it arises in those forms.
And it does not exist in the way that it appears.

That which is the seeing of an object is non-erroneous with respect to it; it is free from existence because of the absence of grasped and grasper, and it is free from non-existence because the object exists [in its ultimate nature].

Because of the existence of the error consisting in the appearance of that [object], the mental attention consisting of discursive speech (*jalpamanaskāra*), which is cultivated by that [error], has that as its basis;
this is non-erroneousness regarding mental attention, which is the cause for the manifestation of duality. (V.16)

The mental engagement consisting of discursive thought (*jalpamanaskāra*), which is thoroughly permeated by the discourse of the grasped and the grasper, becomes the basis for that conceptualization of the grasped and the grasper; this is non-erroneousness with respect to mental engagement. In what kind of mental engagement? In that which is the cause for the manifestation of the grasped and the grasper. For that mental engagement consisting of discursive thought should be understood as the basis for the conceptualization of the grasped and the grasper because it is thoroughly permeated by the notions of verbal expression. Furthermore, the non-existence and existence of the object is considered to be like an illusion and so forth.
Thus, there is no deviation and no error regarding non-deviation from existence and non-existence (V.17).

That which was just mentioned—the non-existence and existence of the object—is held to be like an illusion; for example, an illusion does not exist as the entity of an elephant and so forth, yet it is not the case that it does not exist at all.

Because that exists merely as an error (bhrānti-mātra). Likewise, the object also does not exist in the manner it appears as the apprehended and the apprehender; yet it is not non-existent either, because it exists merely as an error.

By the word "etcetera" (ādi), examples such as a mirage, a dream, the moon reflected in water, and so forth, should be understood according to their respective applications for the purpose of illustrating the similes of illusion and the like.

Through [the realization of] vision, one perceives the non-dispersal of the mind; that non-dispersal is non-perversion, because by it the mind does not disperse toward existence or non-existence. The fact that everything is merely a name is for the sake of the non-occurrence of all conceptual constructions.

Non-perversion regarding specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) is the knowledge that all this— from the eye and visible forms up to the mind and mental objects— is merely name (*nāmamātra*). This knowledge, which serves as the antidote to all conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*), is non-perversion regarding specific characteristics.
In which particular characteristic? In the ultimate particular characteristic (paramārtha-svalakṣaṇa).
However, from the perspective of conventional reality (saṃvṛti), this is not grasped as being "mere name" (nāmamātra).
Since no phenomenon exists apart from the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), therefore that [realm] is the universal characteristic; and this is non-erroneousness with respect to it.
(V.19) For indeed, no phenomenon whatsoever exists without the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*).
Therefore, the dharmadhātu is the universal characteristic (sāmānyalakṣaṇa) of all phenomena.
Knowledge that it is thus is non-delusion regarding the universal characteristic,
by virtue of neither abandoning nor failing to abandon distorted mental engagement.
Its impurity and its purity, and that is the non-perversion therein.

(V.20) The non-abandonment of perverted mental attention is the impurity of that *dharmadhātu*, and its abandonment is its purity; such knowledge is the non-perversion regarding impurity and purity respectively, because the *dharmadhātu* is pure by nature, like space.
For the duality is adventitious, and that is the absence of error therein;
moreover, because the *dharmadhātu* is naturally pure like space.
Both of these—impurity and subsequent purity—are adventitious;
such knowledge is non-perversion regarding adventitiousness.
(Mvbh 68)

There is neither affliction nor purification of either phenomena or persons, because they do not exist; thus, there is neither fear nor pride. Therefore, this is non-perversion in this regard. (V.22) For there is no affliction of a person, nor purification, nor even of a phenomenon.

Since there is neither a person (*pudgala*) nor a phenomenon (*dharma*), and since for no one is there defilement (*saṃkleśa*) or purification (*vyavadāna*), therefore on the side of defilement there is no loss for anyone, and on the side of purification there is no excellence for anyone; because of this, there would be either fear or pride. This [realization] is the absence of error regarding the state of being without fear and without pride.
[The Ten Vajra-Points:
These ten non-perversions are to be applied respectively to the ten vajra-points.
The ten vajra-points are as follows:
Existence and non-existence are non-perversion;
the basis is likeness to an illusion, non-conceptuality, natural luminosity, affliction, and purification;
and likeness to space, as well as non-deficiency and non-distinction.
The systematic presentation of the body of the vajra-words is by way of their intrinsic nature and their objective referents.
By way of non-conceptuality and by way of objections and their resolution.
Among these, by way of intrinsic nature, there are three intrinsic natures.

The perfected, the imagined, and the dependent are designated by the first three terms respectively, according to their objects. These very [three] are [defined] by way of non-conceptualization: that by which one does not conceptualize—namely, non-conceptual gnosis—and that which one does not conceptualize—namely, intrinsic luminosity.
Therefore, by this, the establishment of the object of knowledge and the knowledge itself should be understood in due order:
namely, by means of the three natures, by way of non-conceptuality,
and by way of objections and their refutations.
Regarding the remaining words, this objection arises:
if these phenomena characterized by the imagined and dependent natures do not exist,
how are they perceived?
If the luminous nature of phenomena (*dharmāṇāṃ prakṛtiprabhāsvaratā*) were not found to exist, it would be untenable;
therefore, he resolves this by means of the simile of an illusion.

Just as that which is produced by magic does not exist [in reality] yet is perceived, if the luminous nature of phenomena exists, how could there first be affliction (*saṃkleśa*) and subsequently purification (*vyavadāna*)?
The resolution to this is as follows:
affliction and purification are to be understood through the analogy of space.
Just as space is pure by nature yet becomes afflicted, so it is here.
And it is said that "it is purified":
if, upon the arising of immeasurable Buddhas, there is the pacification of the afflictions of immeasurable sentient beings,
then how is it that there is neither the total cutting off of saṃsāra nor an increase in nirvāṇa?
The resolution for that [objection] is by way of its being neither deficient nor superior,
because the realm of sentient beings (*sattvadhātu*) and the side of purification (*vyavadānapakṣa*) are immeasurable.
This is the second establishment of the body.
Wherein and what [is] delusion, and from what [it arises]; what is non-delusion and wherein [it occurs]; the fruits of delusion and non-delusion, and the ultimate limit of those two.
The non-perversion regarding existence and non-existence, the basis, the simile of illusion,
non-conceptuality, and luminosity by nature— these indeed always exist.
Defilement and purification, likewise the likeness to space,
and neither deficiency nor excess— these indeed are the ten vajra-points.
The practice in accordance with the Dharma has been explained.
What is the practice regarding the avoidance of the two extremes? It is that which is taught as the Middle Way in the *Ratnakūṭa*.
By the avoidance of which extremes is this [middle way] to be understood?
Both difference and identity are extremes, as are those of the non-Buddhists and the śrāvakas.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of extremes regarding persons and phenomena: the extreme of superimposition and the extreme of denial. (V.23)

The extremes of the discordant factors and their antidotes, those designated as eternalism and nihilism, and those regarding the grasped and the grasper, as well as affliction and purification—each being twofold and threefold—and the extreme of dualistic conceptualization: this is considered to be sevenfold. (V.24)
In the presence or absence of existence, in the state of being pacified or in the act of pacifying, in fear or in the absence of fear;
in the grasped and the grasper, in correctness and error, and in activity or its lack. V.25 (Mvbh 70)
If they were simultaneous with non-arising, that would be the extreme of the two conceptual alternatives (V.26).
In that regard,
the view that the self is distinct from form and the other aggregates is one extreme.

The notion of "oneness" is an extreme; for the purpose of avoiding that, there is the middle way, which is neither the contemplation of a self nor, up to, the contemplation of a person. For when there is the view of a self, there arises [the identification] "the soul is this body."

The view that the soul is one thing and the body another is the extreme of the non-Buddhists; that form is eternal is the extreme of the Śrāvakas; and that it is impermanent is [also] the extreme of the Śrāvakas.
In order to avoid those [extremes], there is the middle way (*madhyamā pratipad*), which is neither the contemplation of form and so forth as permanent nor the contemplation of them as impermanent.

"Self" is the extreme of superimposition (*samāropa*) regarding the person (*pudgala*); "selflessness" (*nairātmya*) is the extreme of denial (*apavāda*), because it denies even that which exists as a conceptual designation (*prajñaptisat*). In order to avoid those [extremes], there is the middle way, which is the non-conceptual knowledge (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) that is the middle between self and selflessness.
To say "the mind exists" is the extreme of superimposition regarding phenomena; to say "it does not exist" is the extreme of denial.
For the purpose of avoiding these, there is the middle way, wherein there is neither mind, nor volition, nor intellect, nor consciousness.
To say that unwholesome and other such phenomena are "defilement" is the extreme of the adverse side.

The view that "the wholesome and so forth are purification" is the extreme of the antidote; for the sake of abandoning that, there is the middle way, which is the non-approach, non-proclamation, and non-expression of these two extremes.

To say "it exists" regarding those very persons and phenomena is the extreme of eternalism, and to say "it does not exist" is the extreme of nihilism; for the sake of abandoning those, the middle way is that which is the middle between these two extremes. Furthermore, ignorance is an extreme, as are the grasped and the grasper.
Thus, ignorance and the formative forces are one extreme, and their antidote—the unconditioned—is the other;

likewise, up to old age and death, there are the extremes of the grasped and the grasper, and the extremes of the cessation of those [factors] as either grasped or grasper, as well as the path by which they are ceased.
In this way, there is the extreme of the grasped and the grasper.

It is twofold, distinguished by the division of the dark and light sides; for the purpose of abandoning that, the middle way is the practice [realizing] that "knowledge and ignorance are non-dual. Thus, in detail, because knowledge, ignorance, and so forth lack the nature of grasped object and grasping subject, there is threefold defilement: the defilement of afflictions (*kleśa-saṃkleśa*), [the defilement of karma, and the defilement of birth].
There is the defilement of karma and the defilement of birth.
Among these, the defilement of afflictions is threefold.
Views consist of the signs of passion, hatred, and delusion, as well as the aspiration for rebirth;
their antidotes are the knowledge of emptiness, the knowledge of signlessness, and the knowledge of wishlessness.
Then there is the defilement of karma.
The formative activity of wholesome and unwholesome karma, the antidote to which is the non-formative activity of gnosis;
the defilement of birth, which is the arising of rebirth; and for one who has been born, the moment-to-moment arising of the mind and mental factors.
Furthermore, the continuity of rebirth has as its antidote the non-arising of knowledge, the non-production of knowledge, and the lack of intrinsic nature of knowledge.
The removal of these three kinds of affliction is purification;
therein, [it is achieved] by means of the emptiness of knowledge and so forth.

The phenomena such as the emptiness of the objects of knowledge are not made into emptiness and so forth by these three kinds of affliction, as the case may be; for emptiness and the rest exist by their very nature, because the *dharmadhātu* is by nature undefiled. Therefore, if one conceptualizes that the *dharmadhātu* is either afflicted or purified, this is an extreme.
This is for the purpose of avoiding this extreme, since there is neither affliction nor purification for that which is by nature undefiled.
The middle way is that which does not make phenomena empty by means of emptiness,
but rather [recognizes] that phenomena themselves are empty, and so forth.

Another sevenfold [classification] consists of the two extremes of conceptualization, as follows: conceptualization regarding existence is an extreme; conceptualization regarding non-existence is an extreme, because of the imagination that "the person exists for whose destruction emptiness [is taught]," or that "even selflessness does not exist."
Therefore, for the sake of avoiding these two extremes of conceptual construction, there is this Middle Way.

Indeed, emptiness is not for the purpose of destroying the person; rather, emptiness itself is empty—the emptiness of the prior limit, the emptiness of the posterior limit, and so forth, as detailed at length.

Conceptualization regarding tranquility (*śāmya*) is an extreme; conceptualization regarding the act of calming (*śamana*) is the non-extreme. Because one fears emptiness through the conceptual construction of something to be abandoned and its abandonment, the simile of space is given for the purpose of avoiding these two extremes of conceptualization. Conceptualization regarding that which is to be feared (*trāsya*) is an extreme, and likewise, conceptualization regarding fear itself arises from fearing imagined forms and so forth.
Out of fear of suffering, for the sake of avoiding these two extremes of conceptual construction, there is the simile of the painter;

whereas the previous simile concerned the Śrāvakas, this one concerns the Bodhisattvas. Conceptual construction regarding the object of apprehension (*grāhya*) is an extreme, and conceptual construction regarding the subject of apprehension (*grāhaka*) is also an extreme; for the sake of avoiding these two extremes of conceptual construction, there is the simile of the magician.
For the knowledge of the non-existence of objects is produced by the knowledge of representation-only;
and that very knowledge of the non-existence of objects causes that same knowledge of representation-only to cease.
Because representation is impossible in the absence of an object—this is the point of similarity here.

Even regarding correctness, conceptualization is an extreme; even regarding falsity, there is the extreme for one who conceptualizes the investigation of reality as either correctness or falsity. To avoid these two extremes, there is the analogy of fire from two pieces of wood.

Just as fire, which does not possess the characteristics of fire, is produced from two pieces of wood, and once produced, consumes those very two pieces of wood, so too is it with the investigation of reality as it is (*yathābhūtapratyavekṣā*), which does not possess the characteristics of incorrectness.
The noble faculty of wisdom, characterized by rightness (*samyaktva*), arises; once arisen, it cultivates that very same discernment of reality (*bhūtapratyavekṣā*).

This is the point of similarity here. Furthermore, even though the discernment of reality is not characterized by rightness, it does not possess the characteristic of falsity (*mithyātva*) because it is conducive to rightness.
Even while engaged in activity, conceptualization (*vikalpa*) is an extreme.

The simile of the oil lamp is intended to avoid these two extremes of conceptual construction: either imagining that knowledge performs an intentional action even when it is inactive, or imagining its lack of efficacy.

Even if there is no arising, conceptualization is an extreme; likewise, even if they are simultaneous, if one imagines either the non-arising of the antidote or the long duration of affliction itself, for the sake of avoiding these two extremes of conceptualization, there is the second illustration of the oil lamp.
The practice for avoiding the two aforementioned extremes has been explained.
[Now follows] the distinguished and the undistinguished practice.
What is the distinguished and the undistinguished practice?
It should be understood that [the practice] is both distinguished and undistinguished across the ten stages.
On whichever stage a particular perfection is most predominant, it is distinguished therein; yet, because it is fully realized everywhere on all stages, it is undistinguished.
Thus, the supremacy of practice has been explained.
[3. Supreme Nature of the Object] What is the supreme nature of the object (*ālambanānuttarya*)? It is:
the formal establishment, likewise the realm, that which is to be accomplished, the means of accomplishment, and retention. V.27
Determination, maintenance, penetration, expansion, progress,
and serenity are considered the objects of excellence. (V.28)
Thus, there are these twelve kinds of objects of focus (*ālambana*): namely,

the object of focus consisting in the formal establishment of the designation of phenomena (*dharmaprajñapti*), the object of focus that is the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), the object of focus that is the goal to be accomplished (*sādhya*), the object of focus that is the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*), the object of focus that is retention (*dhāraṇa*), and the object of focus that is definitive determination (*avadhāraṇa*).
The object of sustained attention,
the object of penetration,
and the object of expansion.

The objects of focus are: the object of entry, the object of serenity, and the object of excellence. Among these, the first consists of those dharmas such as the perfections (pāramitā) which are established.
The second is suchness; the third and fourth are those same two respectively, because through the penetration of the *dharmadhātu*, there is the realization of the *pāramitās* and other dharmas.
The fifth is the objective support of the knowledge consisting of hearing (*śrutamaya-jñāna*);
the sixth—

The seventh [retention] is due to the retention of what has been understood through that consisting of reflection; the eighth is due to the individual retention of that consisting of cultivation on the first stage, namely,
the path of seeing.
The ninth [type of knowledge] pertains to the path of cultivation up to the seventh stage;
the tenth pertains to that very same [stage], being the mundane and supramundane paths,
due to the realization of the dharmas according to their specific modes.

The eleventh [object] occurs on the eighth stage, and the twelfth on the three stages beginning with the ninth; for those same first two [objects] receive their respective designations as objects in each of those particular states. The object has been explained.
[4. Unsurpassedness of Realization] What is realization? It consists of non-deficiency, non-rejection, non-distraction, and fulfillment.
Arising, firm establishment, flexibility, non-abiding,
freedom from obscuration, and its uninterrupted attainment—
thus, this is the tenfold attainment. (V.29)
In this regard, the non-deficiency of conditions is the full realization of the lineage;
the non-rejection of the Mahāyāna is the full realization of resolute belief.
The non-distraction from the Hīnayāna is the full attainment of the generation of the thought of awakening;
the fulfillment of the perfections is the full attainment of practice;
and the arising of the noble path is the full attainment of entering the state of certainty.
The firm rooting of the roots of virtue through long-term cultivation is the attainment of the ripening of sentient beings.
The adaptability of the mind is the attainment of the purification of the field.
Not abiding in either saṃsāra or nirvāṇa is the attainment of receiving the prophecy of the irreversible stage, because one does not turn back from either saṃsāra or nirvāṇa.
Freedom from obscuration is the realization of the stage of a Buddha;
the non-cessation of that is the realization of the manifestation of enlightenment.
[Śāstranāmavyākhyāna]
Thus,
this treatise is called the *Madhyavibhāga* because it elucidates the Middle Way; it is also the *Madhyāntavibhāga* because it elucidates both the middle and the two extremes.
It is either the middle [section] devoid of the beginning and end,
or it is precisely that which has a hidden, essential meaning;
this is because, respectively, it is beyond the scope of logic and cannot be refuted by opponents.
And it is of great purpose, because it concerns both oneself and others;
it is for the sake of all.
Because it pertains to the three vehicles,

V.30 (Mvbh 76)
Because it brings about the abandonment of the obscurations of afflictions and the knowable,
this is the summary meaning of its unsurpassed nature.
In brief, there are three kinds of unsurpassedness:
practice, the basis of practice, and the fruit of practice. And as for that practice, it is of such a nature that it is supreme, and by which—
"Attention to the Dharma of the Mahāyāna according to how it has been taught" (V.
7ab), and so forth;

"in what manner" means by which mode [it is transformed], being transformed into non-distraction through the cultivation of calm abiding (*śamatha*) and transformed into non-perversion through the cultivation of insight (*vipaśyanā*).
And for what purpose: for the sake of departure by means of the middle way; and wherein:
in the ten stages (*bhūmi*), which are both distinguished and undistinguished.
The summary meaning of the non-perversions is as follows:
through non-perversion regarding the letter, one penetrates the sign of calm abiding;
through non-perversion regarding the meaning, one penetrates the sign of insight.
Through non-perversion regarding mental attention, one avoids the cause of perversion; through non-perversion regarding non-distraction, one correctly grasps its sign;
and through non-perversion regarding specific characteristics, one cultivates the non-conceptual path as its antidote.
Through non-erroneousness regarding the general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), one penetrates the nature of purification (*vyavadānaprakṛti*).
Through non-erroneousness regarding mental attention to impurity and purity, one discerns whether the obscurations to that [nature] have been abandoned or not.
Through non-erroneousness regarding their adventitious nature (*āgantukatva*), one understands affliction and purification as they truly are.
Through the reversal of fear and pride, one emerges into the state free from obscurations.
This is the fifth chapter, the Determination of Unsurpassability.
(Mvbh 77) The Madhyāntavibhāga is completed.
May whatever merit exists from composing this commentary lead to the arising of merit for the great world,
and to the arising of wisdom, so that there may be great exaltation.
And may the world attain the three types of enlightenment before long.
Thus [it is said].
The Commentary on the Verses Distinguishing the Middle from the Extremes is completed.
The work of the venerable teacher Vasubandhu.
